fields.explanation: Simple cross-origin requests were always sendable; what the same-origin policy withholds is the response. Reflecting the caller's Origin and adding Access-Control-Allow-Credentials tells the browser to hand that authenticated response to the calling page, so any site the victim visits can read their data. It does not switch off the same-origin policy globally, and requests without an Origin are not the problem. This is why you allow an explicit list of origins, and why the wildcard is rejected outright when credentials are involved.

fields.hint: Ask what a breach notification would actually have to cover, rather than what a settings screen or a schema says.

problems: hint says the test is whether the data can single out a person, which is the key (data that identifies a person) reworded
evidence: knowledge: personal data is information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person, directly or in combination with other data, not a fixed list of official identifiers
notes: Explanation's closing contrast between an aggregate row and a single support ticket is accurate and useful.

fields.hint: Encryption and aggregation are things you do to data you already hold. Ask what this principle says about holding it at all.

problems: hint names the two halves of the answer and then asks which option answers both, which eliminates every alternative
evidence: knowledge: data minimization limits collection and retention to what a stated purpose requires, which is why a retention schedule is part of the control
knowledge: encryption reduces the impact of holding data without reducing what is held
notes: Explanation correctly treats aggregation as one technique rather than the principle.

fields.hint: Ask which layer performs the decryption, and who is already on the right side of it.

problems: hint offers someone holding the media as the first branch of its binary, which is the key almost word for word
evidence: knowledge: encryption at rest protects against loss of the storage medium; an application or database session that is already authenticated reads through the decrypting layer
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html - keys must be held and controlled separately from the data they protect
notes: Explanation does not present encryption at rest as sufficient, which is the trap this item exists to catch.

fields.hint: Transparency is not the same as publication, and a policy document is not a right. Ask what a person can actually demand.

problems: hint asks which capability serves that person and only that person, which leaves just one option standing
evidence: knowledge: GDPR gives data subjects rights of access, rectification and erasure over their own personal data, subject to conditions and to overriding legal retention duties
notes: Explanation is careful that erasure is not absolute and that identity verification belongs in the workflow.

fields.hint: Think past the server where the line was written. Ask what else holds a copy of it a month later.

problems: hint enumerates the file, the aggregator, the backup and the dashboard, which is the key and most of the explanation handed over in advance
evidence: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html - secrets must never be logged; implement either an encryption or masking approach to avoid logging plaintext secrets
knowledge: log lines are copied into aggregation services, their backups and shared dashboards for the whole retention window
notes: Explanation's closing example, logging a user id instead of an email address, answers the lost-context distractor directly.

fields.hint: Ask what would have to be true for re-identification to be impossible for everyone, not just for you.

problems: hint asks whether a key or lookup table still exists, which is the key (whoever holds the mapping) restated
evidence: knowledge: under GDPR, pseudonymised data that can be attributed to a person using additional information remains personal data, while genuinely anonymous information falls outside the regime
knowledge: anonymization requires that re-identification not be reasonably possible, including by combining the set with other data
notes: Explanation gets the legal direction right, which is the trap the last distractor sets.

evidence: knowledge: incident response contains and preserves evidence before eradication, because scope and notification depend on the forensic record
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html - 9.2 Remediation: the primary goal of incident response is rapid response and containment
notes: Hint characterizes the consequences of two wrong instincts without identifying which options they are, so the learner still has to map them.

fields.hint: Ask who can reach a snapshot taken six months ago, and whether anyone would notice them doing it.

problems: hint says the protection around the data usually is not identical, which is the key (outside its access controls and monitoring) reworded
evidence: knowledge: backups are complete copies of production data that commonly live in another account, region or medium with weaker access control and thinner monitoring
https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html - 2.9 Downtime, Break-glass, Backup and Restore treats backup handling as its own control surface
notes: Explanation is right that restore authorization is a separate control, so encryption is not presented as sufficient.

fields.hint: A scanner can only find what was built. Ask which failures never show up as a bug in the code.

evidence: knowledge: a private network is a location rather than an identity, so perimeter-only authentication grants whatever gets inside
knowledge: transport encryption proves confidentiality of the channel, and proves the caller's identity only when a client certificate is verified

fields.question: Which security-testing plan is the most defensible for a production web service?

evidence: knowledge: review finds logic and authorization mistakes scanners do not model, scanners give repeatable breadth, dependency checks cover third-party code, and penetration testing chains weaknesses into a path
knowledge: unit tests written by the implementer inherit the assumptions that produced the defect
